course_description: This course introduces students to the key questions, concepts, approaches, and problems in African Diaspora Studies. It centers the varied histories, experiences, ideas, and creativity of people of African descent around the world. Exploring the changing meanings of Africa and Blackness across time, the course examines the formation of race in different contexts. Students analyze how race, ethnicity, gender, sexuality, kinship, class, age, and geography shape culture, ritual, ideology, and politics through an interdisciplinary lens. Prerequisite: None.

course_description: See ARH-235. This course is a survey of Black art and visual culture, with a focus on modern and contemporary art in the United States and among the African diaspora globally. Our explorations of Black visualities includes topics such as artistic responses to race and racism, transnational connections among artists, writers and intellectuals, African diasporic religious practices, Afro-Futurism, and the politics of popular culture, among others. Prerequisites: ARH-103 or ADS-101.

course_description: Special Topic: Africa's Islands, Archipelagic. Contrary to the popular colonial logic, neither the African continent nor its islands are remote. The island of Zanzibar and the Indian Ocean-facing regions of Africa have long been places where African, Arab, Indian, and Persian lives have converged. This course reads that Swahili world-shaped by and shaping monsoon trade, slavery, and empire-through history, fiction, ecology, and embodied traditions, setting Zanzibar beside Mauritius in recent scholarship. The course includes embedded travel to Zanzibar. Prerequisite: Second-year standing. system_requisites: TUT-100 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Special Topic: Soccer and the African Diaspora. Cross-list HIS-295. Soccer was first introduced in Africa in the nineteenth century at the height of European colonialism. Despite this context, soccer in Africa and among the African diaspora has taken on a life of its own worthy of study. This course traces how soccer evolved from a tool of colonial discipline to a site of anti-colonial resistance. We will examine how soccer (as sport, community, and industry) constitutes an analytic tool for understanding how African diaspora communities engaged imperialism, nationalism, decolonization, and identity. Prerequisite: TUT-100

system_requisites: None
catalog_notes: Description says: Second-year standing. System Requisites field says None.
course_description: Special Topic: Tuberculosis and Global Health. Also listed as SMS-295. Tuberculosis (TB) is a leading infectious disease cause of death in the world, with over 1 million deaths per year, and with the greater burden carried by sub-Saharan Africa, South and Southeast Asia. In this 7-weeks (2 cr.) course, we will explore TB's biology, epidemiology, its historical and social context both in the African global diaspora. Prerequisite: Second-year standing.

system_requisites: None
catalog_notes: Description says: Second-year standing. System Requisites field says None.
course_description: Special Topic: The Birth of American Medicine: Race and Biology Also listed as SMS-295. In America's colonial past, the study of anatomy was intimately intertwined with the use of enslaved bodies. In this 2-cr course, we explore the social history of race and medicine and consider the contributions of Black bodies to Human Anatomy and their role in the development of American medicine. We critically interrogate the ethics and use of Black bodies in medical education. We investigate the persistence of racialized perceptions, research, and practices in clinical medicine. Prerequisite: Second-year standing.

system_requisites: TUT-100 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Special Topic: Postcolonial African Literature in Translation. Also listed as HUM-295 and SAM-295. In this course, we will read some of the most vibrant French-language literature from the African continent in English translation, including foundational "classics" and the contemporary novels of our times, retracing some of the hopes, struggles, and issues that have marked postcolonial Africa. Away from stereotypical and incomplete images and reports, we will delve into the creative potential of fiction to help us think about memory, loss, feminism, family, migration, and more. Prerequisite: TUT-100

course_description: An examination of selected beliefs and values that have been central to the shaping of American life and culture. Core values such as equality, individualism, success, freedom, a sense of special mission, pastoralism, and others treated in topical units that range over the totality of American experience. Prerequisite: none. SCOTT

system_requisites: HIS-100, or second-year standing - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: See HIS-215. Students in this course will examine the creation and expansion of U.S popular culture in the nineteenth century as they focus on diverse cultural forms: dime novels, newspapers, music, sports, cartoons, theater, minstrel shows, magazines, etc. The course will focus particularly on how ideas and structures of race, class, and gender were changed and reinforced by American popular culture and will consider theoretical issues involved in the study of popular culture. Prerequisite: HIS-100 or second-year standing. PURCELL

system_requisites: AMS-130, ART-155, or FMS-155 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Also listed as FMS-280. This course examines photography's role in the production of authoritative knowledge about the human body in the U.S. - including by advancing pseudoscientific theories of racial hierarchies, propagating ethnic stereotypes, informing medical diagnoses of the disabled body, delimiting aesthetic ideals for gendered life, and creating spectacles of violence against Black bodies. We will also look at how artists and activists have used the camera as a tool of resistance to resignify marginalized bodies with political power. Prerequisite: AMS-130, ART-155, or FMS-155. REZNICK

system_requisites: AMS 130 and one 4 credit AMS 200-level course - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Advanced Special Topic: Captsone Seminar. The American Studies Capstone Seminar is the culminating intellectual experience for concentrators, in which each student undertakes an ambitious, individualized research project reflecting their distinct interests within American Studies. Students formulate a focused research question of consequence to the study of American culture; assemble and critically evaluate an archive of primary sources; and situate their project within relevant scholarly and theoretical conversations in American Studies and adjacent fields. Prerequisite: AMS-130 and one 200-level AMS course.

system_requisites: None
course_description: Human Migrations. How has migration shaped human history? This class introduces students to the four subfields of anthropology (linguistic anthropology, cultural anthropology, archaeology, and biological anthropology) by exploring human mobility from our origins as humans to the present-day. We will look at evidence of movement and gene flow in early modern humans, investigate the benefits of nomadic hunting and gathering over agriculture and sedentism, explore how language and material culture can help us trace ancient migrations, and examine the contemporary lives of transnational migrants who move between their homeland and another country. The class format will include lectures, discussion, and in-class labs. Prerequisite: None.

system_requisites: None
course_description: Empire and Class-ification. This introductory course invites students to consider anthropology as a set of power-laden analytic tools. How do archaeology, biological, linguistic, and sociocultural anthropology deploy interdisciplinary techniques for studying today's most pressing problems from ecological devastation to racialized hierarchy? How are the discipline's traditional "4 fields" embedded in histories of imperialism, capitalism, and attendant discontent? Empirical classification-e.g., of primate behavior or material remains-is both at the heart of anthropological practice and also a deeply political endeavor. Assignments focused on ethnography and multimedia will prepare majors for continued exploration and valuable inquiry, including in non-academic professional careers. Prerequisite: None.

system_requisites: None
course_description: Kinship and Human Nature introduces students to the four fields of anthropology through the study of kinship. Examining family, relatedness, and social ties across cultures and across time, the course explores how kinship has shaped human evolution, language, material culture, and social organization. Drawing on biological anthropology, archaeology, linguistic anthropology, and cultural anthropology, students learn how kinship structures cooperation, identity, and inequality in human societies. Prerequisite: None. STAFF.

course_description: Introductory Special Topic: Totally Bananas! The Liberal Arts in a Fruit. Also listed as SST-195. This course investigates bananas through a Liberal Arts lens. Students will examine different aspects of this fruit through the fields of Anthropology, Biology, Economics, Gender Studies, History, Literature, Political Science, and the visual and performing arts. Two themes will emerge in the course. First, bananas constitute a commodity that has shaped economic and political relationships globally. Second, bananas have varied cultural meanings- both as a food and a cultural icon. This course involves travel during spring break as well as summer 2027. course_description: Reviews various cultural anthropology approaches to understanding human/environment interactions through ethnographic case studies of small-scale societies from distinct environmental regions. How do "extreme" environments affect human adaption? How are cultures shaped by their efforts to acquire food and by their conceptualizations of the natural environment? How are small-scale cultures and  their environments affected by increasing integration into the world system (e.g., through globalization). Prerequisite: Anthropology 104, or Global Development Studies 111; with grade S, C, or better. ROPER.

system_requisites: ANT-104 and at least one 200-level Anthropology course - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: A survey of the history of anthropological theory from the Enlightenment to the present. Prerequisites: Anthropology 104 and at least one 200-level anthropology course. STAFF.

description_prerequisite: Anthropology 104, or upper-level (200 or 300) archaeology course, with grade S, C, or better
system_requisites: ANT-104 or upper-level archaeology course, with grade S, C, or better - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: How do archaeologists know where to dig? What techniques are used to date an artifact or archaeological site? What theoretical approaches do archaeologists use to interpret a site? This course provides an overview of the field and laboratory methods that archaeologists use to study past societies and an introduction to archaeological theory. Through readings and hands-on activities, students will be exposed to a range of archaeological methods such as survey, stratigraphic excavation, stone tools analysis, ceramic analysis, zooarchaeology, and archaeobotanical analysis. Prerequisite: Anthropology 104, or upper-level (200 or 300) archaeology course, with grade S, C, or better. STAFF.

course_description: See Sociology 291. An overview of the research process in sociology and the social sciences, with emphasis on problems of epistemology, research design, techniques of sampling, methods of data collection, principles of measurement, basic methods of data analysis, and ethical considerations. This course will explore these topics through hands-on experiences including guided work on research methods through lab exercises. Prerequisite: Sociology 111 or Anthropology 104, and one 200-level sociology course and Social Studies 115, Statistics 209 (preferred), or Mathematics/Statistics 336; with grades S, C, or better. PANDAIAN, QUINSAAT.

course_description: Special Topic: New Balkan Studies at Empire's Edge: Beyond Beaches, Dragons, and Powder Kegs. Europe's Balkan edge offers a valuable lens onto studying myriad pressing political issues including imperialism, fascism, language ideology, anti-nationalist solidarity, mediated fantasy and dangerous cultural stereotype. Since the 19th century, fears of Balkan "powderkegs" have justified outsider intervention and erosions of local sovereignty. Increasingly since the Yugoslav Wars ended in the 1990s, sandy Adriatic beaches and medieval coastal walls have offered bourgeois tourist-consumers escapist dreamworlds. How have regional scholars, activists, and mediamakers reimagined these powerful perceptions? Students will be traveling during spring break. Prerequisite: A course in the social studies division except PHE-100 or 101. Students interested in this course will need to complete an application by October 5, 2026 in addition to doing the normal registration process. course_description: This class will explore the theories and methods that archaeologists have used to study the material record of racialized groups in the United States. Course readings will cover early archaeological investigations of racialized communities, how archaeologists have worked with descendant communities, the impacts of colonization, debates around acculturation and assimilation models, the archaeology of racialization, and studies of diaspora and transnationalism. Prerequisite: previous completion on or concurrent enrollment in: ANT-263, ANT-290, ANT-388, ANT-295 or ANT-395 if counting towards Archaeology subfield.

system_requisites: ANT-280 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Advanced Special Topic: Anthropology of Children and Youth. In this seminar, students will examine childhood and youth from an anthropological perspective. Students will learn about the history of anthropology's engagement with the topic, as well as its main contemporary debates such as the social construction of childhood and adolescence, childrearing practices around the world, growth, agency, schooling, child labor, child rights, and structural inequality. Students will conduct a field research project and analyze their own childhood and youth experiences. Prerequisites: ANT-280

system_requisites: ARB-101 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: This course is designed primarily as a continuation of Arabic 101. Emphasizes the development of oral-aural skills and of reading comprehension by providing communicative practice and attention to cultural context. Prerequisite: Arabic 101 or by placement. YOUSSEF.

system_requisites: ARB-221 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Conducted in Arabic. Focuses on the development of written and oral skills. Emphasizes vocabulary acquisition, discussion, and composition through the exploration of literary texts and contemporary media materials. Prerequisite: Arabic 221. YOUSSEF.

system_requisites: None
course_description: A thematic and cross-cultural study of art and architecture as expressions of diverse social, intellectual, religious, and aesthetic values, primarily in Western societies since antiquity, with reference to certain East Asian and African traditions. Emphasis on developing critical skills. Use of Grinnell College Art Collection. Prerequisite: none. STAFF.

system_requisites: Second-year standing - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Introduction to Museum Studies explores a number of issues of museum history, theory, and practice, using public scholarship and research along with intensive class discussions and visits to area museums. The content is directly applicable to students in art history, anthropology, education, history, studio art and sciences. Prerequisite: Second-year standing. BALEY

system_requisites: ARH-103 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Also listed as EAS-213. This class explores themes of gender and sexuality in the arts of China, Japan, and Korea from the beginning of the Common Era to the present day. This class does not aim to be comprehensive but will rather focus on a series of examples that allow insights into culturally specific moments. We will be looking at a variety of media and will interrogate the diverse cultural contexts in which this art was produced and consumed. Prerequisites: ARH-103.

system_requisites: None
course_description: See Classics 250. A study of the major monuments and artifacts of ancient Etruria and Rome; their relationship to the political and cultural history; the Roman borrowing and adoption of Greek forms as well as original expression in art and architecture. Roman artistic exchange with other cultures of Europe, Africa, and Asia. Prerequisite: none. M. CUMMINS.

system_requisites: ARH 103 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: This course offers a survey of developments in modern architecture from the 19th century to the mid-20th century, with a focus on globalization. We discuss the aesthetic, political and social contexts of architecture, including colonialism, urbanization, industrialization, authoritarianism and nationalism. We will use visual materials (floor plans, renderings, photographs, etc.), texts by architects, scholars and critics, and local/regional examples of architecture to examine the built environment, architectural movements, urban planning, landscape design and architectural technologies. Prerequisites: ARH 103 RIVERA

system_requisites: Second-year standing - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Special Topic: Reframing Medieval Art, Blessed to Bawdy. Using the recently published textbook on medieval art, co-authored by Anne Harris, this course reframes traditional surveys of art and architecture (750-1450) by applying current theoretical approaches to a broad spectrum of artistic production ranging from cathedrals to combs created across Europe and parts of Africa and West Asia. In this course, you will develop your own research in a paper, blog, or medieval-inspired design project. Prerequisite: Second-year standing.

system_requisites: None

course_description: Special Topic: Transnational Women's Cinema. See ARH-295. In this course, we will unpack "women's cinema" by engaging with how feminist theories, politics, and practices coincide with transnational film production, circulation, and distribution in films made by women filmmakers. We will consider topics such as auteur theory, spectatorship, and representation as we watch films across genres. We will examine the feminist worldbuilding and modes of allyship in women's cinema while paying attention to factors such as race, sexuality, class, caste, nation, and ethnicity. Prerequisite: Second-year standing.

description_prerequisite: ARH 103 and one 200-level ARH course and third-year standing
system_requisites: ARH-103 and one 200-level ARH course and third-year standing - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: This course studies the theory and methods of art history. We will explore historical and philosophical approaches as well as contemporary methods. The point is to think through how and why we approach art and architecture the way we do and to learn to do so more conscientiously and fruitfully. Prerequisite: ARH 103 and one 200-level ARH course and third-year standing. ANGER

system_requisites: Second-year standing - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Advanced Special Topic: Cinema Spectatorship and Exhibition. Also listed as FMS-395. This course analyzes theories of the cinema spectator, the spectator's relationship to the screen, and the formulation of the spectator through specific media technologies. Students study psychoanalytic, phenomenological, and affective approaches to spectatorship, examine the history of movie exhibition, and consider how individual technologies (television, video, YouTube) shape the spectator's experience and identity. Throughout the course, students develop understandings of spectatorship through written reflections, curating screenings, and developing both individual and group exhibition designs. Prerequisite: Second-year standing.

system_requisites: None
course_description: Introduction to the Studio is a beginning level studio course designed to introduce and ground students in core principles of art making in a rigorous, hands on studio. These principles will be taught though a series of practical exercises using traditional and digital tools. Emphasis will be placed on developing skills, knowledge of materials, methods of observation and translation, collaboration, discussion, and creative discipline. Prerequisite: none. STAFF.

system_requisites: None
course_description: An introduction to observational drawing and contemporary drawing practice. Subjects will include architecture, objects, landscape and the figure. Traditional and non traditional media will be explored. Emphasis on technical skill, perceptual development and critical skills. Prerequisite: none. STAFF.

system_requisites: None
course_description: Also listed as FMS-155. This course introduces students to select issues in film studies. Students will learn key vocabulary and concepts of film forms, techniques, and history and develop critical-analysis skills necessary to become informed viewers of a wide variety of historical and contemporary films. Class time will be used for screenings and critical study of major films. Students will produce written critical responses to film, production exercises using consumer tools (smartphones), and a research presentation. Prerequisite: None. TAVARES

system_requisites: Pre-req: ART-111 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: This course will explore techniques and concepts employed by contemporary sculptors. Students will utilize materials from the ephemeral to the permanent to explore issues of space and construction through a series of creative projects. Prerequisite: ART 111. STAFF

system_requisites: Second-year standing - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Also listed as FMS-255-01. This hands-on production course is designed to introduce students to the moving image as a form of contemporary art practice. Students will learn the skills, theories, and concepts used in digital video, participating in all aspects of production, including gathering ideas, writing a project description, storyboarding, shooting, editing, and screening. Students will be exposed to and research a range of moving image artists, gaining an understanding of the history of video art and related forms. Prerequisite: second-year standing. TAVARES

system_requisites: ART-111 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Special Topic: Experimental Ceramics. We will investigate the possibilities of ceramics. We will break away from the perceived limits of the material and find new paths to explore installation, mix media, and performance will be used as ways of making to encourage innovation within the expanding ceramic field. Students read, write, observe, present, experiment and construct within the studio setting to research and develop ceramic sculpture resulting in a small portfolio that reflects each student's inquiry in individual and group work. Prerequisite: ART 111.

system_requisites: ART-111 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Special Topic: Performing the Body. Students will investigate conceptual relationships between language, the body, and time-based media to consider themes surrounding constructed identity and embodied persona. Studio investigations will be guided by artworks and actions stemming from the Fluxus movement of the 1960s and '70s, automatic writing exercises, and contemporary approaches to personal narrative. Creative projects will include wearable sculptures, puppet forms, shadow theater, video, and performance. Class time also consists of readings, discussions, and critiques of student-led creative works. Prerequisite: ART 111.

system_requisites: Twelve credits of 200-level studio art - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: An interdisciplinary studio course designed to introduce students to contemporary artistic practices and concepts. Emphasis is placed on ideation, concept and form integration. Repeastable one time for credit. Prerequisite: twelve credits of 200-level studio art. KAUFMAN.

system_requisites: None
course_description: The goal of this course is to foster continued learning development in students. This learning development is built on theories and concepts from the fields of cognitive and learning psychology, evidence-based learning strategies, and research that examines obstacles to the learning process. Students will research and practice evidence-based strategies and apply them to their existing courses with opportunities for reflection and feedback. Open to all students. 1/2 semester deadlines apply. Prerequisite: None.

course_description: An introduction to chemical properties and biological functions of proteins, nucleic acids, carbohydrates, and lipids. Topics in lecture and lab include purifying and characterizing proteins, enzyme kinetics, and basic energy metabolism. Three lectures and one scheduled lab each week. Prerequisite: Biology 251, Chemistry 221, and completion of or concurrent registration in Chemistry 222. BAILEY, LEVANDOSKI, TRIMMER.

system_requisites: None
course_description: No description available.

system_requisites: None
course_description: "Sex Life of Plants." This course will explore the evolution and ecology of reproduction in flowering plants to develop your understanding of how and why plants reproduce as they do. You'll experience biology as it is practiced, as you learn principles of adaptation, practice the scientific method, and communicate your research findings in the style of professional biologists. Activities will include reading and discussing classic and contemporary scientific literature, completing exercises on the structure and function of plant reproductive features, and conducting and reporting on research projects done in the lab, the greenhouse, and the field. Prerequisite: none. ECKHART.

system_requisites: None
course_description: "Sexy Beast" Why do animals have sex? and in such incredible variety? This course will consider the ways biologists study the causes and consequences of sex in animals at all levels -- from the cellular process of meiosis, to the organismal concept of gender, to mating interactions between individuals and their evolutionary consequences. Students will learn to read and evaluate the primary literature, formulate hypotheses, and carry out independent research projects using a model organism, the bean beetle Callosobruchus maculatus. Students will communicate their results in scientific papers, posters, and oral presentations. Finally, as sexy beasts ourselves, we will consider how our human biases and social assumptions influence the questions asked and their accepted answers. Prerequisite: none. COOPER

system_requisites: None
course_description: Regeneration. In this course we will investigate regeneration using studies from phanaria, fish and axolotl. Based on critical reading of the literature, students will design and carry out independent research projects, analyze and report the results in scientific papers, posters and oral presentation. The class will combine lecture, lab, and discussion. Prerequisite: none. STAFF.

system_requisites: None
course_description: Neurons under Stress:You are born with most of the neurons you will have for the rest of your life. These neurons must be maintained through stress and injury, and when neuronal health fails, behavior changes and neurological disease can arise. How do neurons stay alive for so long? Fruit flies (Drosophila melanogaster) also have neurons that function similarly to those of humans and provide a model system for studying nervous system. In this course, we will investigate how neurons in Drosophila function and how that function is perturbed during stress. Topics addressed will include neuronal signaling, mechanisms of neuronal maintenance, and processes that contribute to neurodegeneration. Students will use genetic and behavioral approaches to study neuronal function. We will also evaluate scientific literature and carry out independent research projects. Students will analyze and communicate their findings through scientific papers, posters, and oral presentations. Prerequisite: None.

system_requisites: TUT-100 and application. Open to first-year students only. - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Special Topic: New and Emerging Infectious Diseases: Of the 108 billion humans who have ever lived, half have died of mosquito-vectored diseases. Indeed, throughout human history and prehistory, infectious diseases have determined the fates of cultures and of nations more than any army or political thrall ever could. This course will examine the fundamental pathogenesis, etiology and epidemiology of infectious diseases of human, plant and animals. It will also examine the geopolitical and social changes those diseases have wrought on human demography, history, economy and destiny. Field excursions will be conducted in South Africa and Alaska.These excursions will occur over spring break and summer 2027. Prerequisite: TUT-100 and application. Open to first-year students only. Students interested in this course will need to complete an application by October 5, 2026 in addition to doing the normal registration process. course_description: Investigations of the cellular and molecular basis of organismal structure and function, including studies of how organisms acquire and expend energy, acquire and transport materials, regulate internal conditions, transmit information, reproduce, develop, grow, and move. Three lectures and one scheduled lab each week. Prerequisite: Biology 150, Chemistry 129, and completion of or concurrent registration in Chemistry 221. STAFF.

Course includes lectures and lab each week. Prerequisite: Biology 251 and Mathematics 124, 125, or 131. STAFF. course_description: Special Topic: Genomes, Generations, and Justice. An interdisciplinary study of the role that biology is playing in our understanding of what it means to be human. We will explore how modern genetic techniques have complemented approaches in the social sciences, providing insights into human evolution, migration, language, and ancestry. We will also consider how science has been used to justify oppression and how modern genetics can be used to identify and counter racial categorization and the genetic determinism often invoked to support judicial and social policies. Prerequisite: BIO-150 and AMS-130, ANT-104, GWS-111, LIN-114 or SOC-111.

course_description: No description available.

system_requisites: BIO-251 and BIO-252 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Biologists increasingly rely on R programming to manage, analyze, visualize, and interpret complex biological data. This course introduces students to R and RStudio through hands-on applications to biological research. Students will develop fundamental programming and data-management skills and learn approaches for data wrangling, visualization, reproducible analysis, and working with statistical, spatial, and genetic data. Through in-class exercises, assignments, scientific literature, and an independent project, students will learn to conduct reproducible analyses, interpret results in a biological context, and communicate their findings effectively. No prior programming experience is required. Prerequisite: BIO-251 and BIO-252.

catalog_notes: Unnamed concurrent requisite in catalog; needs registrar confirmation.
course_description: Genetics is an experimental approach that has been applied to questions in all areas of biology, answering fundamental questions about inheritance, cell mechanics, human disease, and evolutionary change. This course will introduce students to advanced genetic principles and techniques. We will then explore how these techniques have been applied to answer fundamental questions in biology by reading both classic and recent papers from the primary literature that utilize genetic approaches. We will also discuss some of the limitations of genetics as a scientific approach. The laboratory will emphasize multiweek projects using genetic techniques to study biological problems. Two three-hour meetings per week. Prerequisite: Biology 252 or Biological Chemistry 262. PRAITIS.

course_description: An introduction to the cellular and molecular basis of vertebrate immune systems. We will explore the innate and adaptive immune systems including their components and organization and development of the immune responses. This course will build on concepts from cell biology and organic chemistry as we explore key molecular pathways of the immune system, incorporating the critical evaluation of primary literature and case studies of immune dysfunction, along with laboratory research, from design through analysis. Prerequisites: BIO-252 or BCM-262.

system_requisites: BIO-252 - Must be completed prior to taking this course. BIO-373L - Must be taken at the same time as this course.
course_description: This course examines the mechanisms of evolutionary change at both the micro and macroevolutionary scales. Topics include the maintenance of genetic variation, population structure and speciation, molecular evolution, systematic methods and applications, and macroevolution. Prerequisite: Biology 252. STAFF.

system_requisites: BIO-252 or BCM-262 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: An examination of the fundamental principles by which pharmacological agents are produced, work, and used. A major part of the course will explore basic concepts of pharmacokinetics (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion) and pharmacodynamics (mechanisms of drug action, receptor theory, dose response relationships, genetic interactions with drugs). Some common drug classes will be examined to illustrate basic physiological and pharmacological principles. Aspects of drug discovery, development and policy may also be introduced. Three lectures and one scheduled laboratory each week. Prerequisites: BIO-252 or BCM-262.

system_requisites: BIO-252 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Single-Cell Genomics in Neuroscience and Psychiatry. This readings course will explore how single-cell and spatial multi-omic technologies have transformed our understanding of the brain and neuropsychiatric disease. While the course establishes an exploratory baseline using early cellular and epigenetic profiling methods (scRNA-seq, snRNA-seq, scATAC-seq), it also emphasizes techniques that link cellular identity to live physiology, balancing the exploratory atlas-building with functional, mechanism-driven perturbation studies. Students will critically analyze landmark literature spanning from early cellular profiling methods to multimodal applications like Patch-seq, perturbation-driven screens, and single-cell proteomics. Prerequisites: BIO-252. STAFF

system_requisites: BIO-251 or BCM-262. No prior programming experience is required, but preferred. - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Advanced Special Topics: Cellular Senescence: Mechanisms, Disease, and Therapeutics. Cellular senescence is a stable cell-cycle arrest associated with broad changes in cellular function and important roles in aging, disease, development, and tissue repair. This course examines the mechanisms, phenotypes, and physiological roles of senescent cells. Students will use yeast to investigate cellular aging, learn computational approaches including transcriptomics and single-cell RNA sequencing, analyze human datasets using Python, and develop an independent computational research project focused on cellular senescence. Prerequisite: BIO-251 or BCM-262. No programming experience is required, but preferred.

Topics include the role of biocatalysis in synthetic chemistry, its advantages and limitations, and the application of bioretrosynthetic analysis to the design and synthesis of target molecules. Prerequisite: BCM-262.

course_description: In this section of CSC 151, we will ground our study of functional problem solving in media computation. In particular, we will explore mechanisms for representing, making, and manipulating images. We will consider a variety of models of images based on pixels, basic shapes, and objects that draw. The course will be taught using a workshop style: In most class sessions, students will work collaboratively on a series of problems. Includes formal laboratory work. Prerequisite: None. STAFF

system_requisites: CSC-151 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Students in CSC 161 will study imperative problem solving, data representation, and memory management. Additional topics will include assertions and invariants, data abstraction, linked data structures, an introduction to the GNU/Linux operating system, and programming the low-level, imperative language C. The course will utilize a workshop style in which students will frequently work collaboratively on a series of problems. Includes formal laboratory work. Prerequisite: Computer Science 151. STAFF.

system_requisites: CSC-151 and CSC-161 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: An introduction to the ideas and practices of object-oriented computation: message passing, information hiding, classes and interfaces, inheritance, polymorphism, and reflection. The course also includes data structures and the associated algorithms, packages and libraries, exceptions, and the use of an integrated software-development environment. Includes formal laboratory work. Prerequisites: Computer Science 151 and 161. STAFF.

course_description: Also listed as Math 208. How do we "know" that a mathematical or logical statement is correct? What common properties appear among different collections? How might we represent functions, and how can we tell if two functions with different representations are the same? Can we formally describe and understand common diagrams? We consider such questions as we develop both intuition and formal mechanisms for addressing them. Along the way, we explore Boolean logic, proof techniques, sets, structures that include trees and graphs, and more Students who are taking or have previously taken Math 218 may not take Computer Science/Math 208. Prerequisite: Computer Science 151 and Math 124 or 131, and completion of or concurrent registration in Computer Science 161. STAFF.

system_requisites: CSC-161 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Study of both traditional and alternative computer architectures. Introduction to digital logic, microcode, Von Neumann architectures, data representations, fetch/execute model, RISC/CISC, instruction formats and addressing, machine and assembly language, memory architecture and algorithms, I/O architecture, and elements of distributed systems. Includes formal laboratory work. Prerequisite: Computer Science 161. CURTSINGER, WEINMAN.

description_prerequisite: Computer Science 207 and either Mathematics 218 or Computer Science/Mathematics 208
system_requisites: CSC-207 and either MAT-218 or CSC/MAT-208 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Study methods for designing, analyzing, and implementing algorithms and data structures. The course explores formal and precise mechanisms for analyzing efficiency and verifying correctness and both iterative and recursive algorithms. Studies also cover a variety of fundamental algorithms, abstract data types, and data structures. Algorithm design strategies included greedy, divide-and-conquer, exhaustive search, and dynamic programming. Additional topics may include approximation, parallel, or randomized algorithms. Prerequisite: Computer Science 207 and either Mathematics 218 or Computer Science/Mathematics 208. STAFF.

system_requisites: CSC-207 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Provides a foundation for "programming in the large" and developing high-quality software that meets human needs. Introduces the software lifecycle, agile development methods, professional tools, and software design principles. Teams develop software for a community organization, supported by a faculty adviser and an alumni technical mentor. Students develop a substantial code base suitable for inclusion in a professional portfolio and gain experience working with a client. Includes laboratory work.. Prerequisite: CSC-207. ELIOTT, PERLMUTTER.

system_requisites: CSC-324 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

Students will gain experience mentoring and coordinating peers while working with a client. Offered simultaneously with CSC-324. Students in this course serve as the leaders on the CSC-324 projects. Includes laboratory work. Prerequisite: CSC-324. ELIOTT, PERLMUTTER.

system_requisites: CSC-207 and either MAT-218 or CSC/MAT-208 with grades S, C, or better. - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: A formal study of computational devices, their related languages, and the possibility and difficulty of computations. Examples are pushdown automata and Turing machines, context-free languages and recursively enumerable sets, and the halting problem and NP-completeness. Prerequisite: Computer Science 207 and either Mathematics 218 or Computer Science/Mathematics 208, with grades S, C, or better. AUTRY, EIKMEIER OSERA.

description_prerequisite: CSC-207 and CSC-208, MAT-208, or MAT-218
system_requisites: CSC-207 and CSC-208, MAT-208, or MAT-218 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Advanced Special Topic: Modern Programming Language Theory and Design. Type systems can prevent errors like memory-safety violations and data races at compile time. This course introduces programming language theory, including operational semantics, lambda calculi, type safety, and polymorphism, and connects it to modern systems languages like Rust and WebAssembly. Topics include ownership, concurrency, parallelism, type-driven development, and types for resources and protocols. Students implement interpreters and type checkers in Rust, and design and implement a small language as a final project. Prerequisite: CSC-207 and CSC-208, MAT-208, or MAT-218.

system_requisites: Second-year standing - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Special Topic: Data and Power. This class takes a critical perspective on the processes by which data is made, examining the power reflected in and perpetuated by data. What damage is done in chopping up the messy, complicated world to fit into the neat boxes of a spreadsheet? Who benefits from and who is harmed by the construction of a dataset? This course examines these questions from the perspective of an emerging, interdisciplinary field called critical data studies. Prerequisite: Second-year standing.

course_name: Gend and Sex in East Asian Art
system_requisites: ARH-103 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: See ARH-213. This class explores themes of gender and sexuality in the arts of China, Japan, and Korea from the beginning of the Common Era to the present day. This class does not aim to be comprehensive but will rather focus on a series of examples that allow insights into culturally specific moments. We will be looking at a variety of media and will interrogate the diverse cultural contexts in which this art was produced and consumed. Prerequisites: ARH-103.

system_requisites: TUT-100 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Special Topic: German-Jewish Cultural Map of Shanghai and the Sinophone World. See GRM-295. This course examines German-Jewish migration, exile, memory, and cultural exchange in Shanghai and the broader Sinophone world. Drawing on literature, memoirs, maps, photographs, archival sources, museums, and film, students explore how German-speaking Jewish refugees interacted within mainland China and the broader Sinophone societies, including Hong Kong, Taiwan, and Singapore,  and how these histories are remembered and represented. Prerequisites: TUT-100

system_requisites: MAT-124 or 131, second-year standing, and one additional economics course between 205-250 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

We'll also explore symbolic vampirism as shown through the television show What We Do In The Shadows. Throughout the course we will discuss the roles gender, sexuality, ethnicity, class, and power positionality plays in vampire folklore, literature and film. Prerequisite: none. LAVAN.

course_description: Adaptation. In this course about adaptation, we'll investigate why some storytellers are legendary and rife with adaptations (Shakespeare, Alexandre Dumas, Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, Jane Austen, Charles Dickens, Bram Stoker, Mary Shelley, Anne Rice). Using Linda Hutcheon's A Theory of Adaptation, as well as other Adaptation Studies texts, we will ask and answer: Is the book always better?  How does a change in form (graphic novel, podcast, theatre, film, television show) alter our experience of the material? How do modern adaptations update these texts while remaining true to the source material? What does the text lose and/or gain in adaptation? How can we compare/contrast the cultural, social, and historical contextual differences and the ways they guide changes in the adapted source material? For your final project, you will choose a text and create your own adaptation. Prerequisite: 4 credits at the 100-level in English or third-year standing with instructor permission. LAVAN.

Throughout, we'll trace recurring themes like encounters with the divine and the marvelous, the changing conditions of textual production and reading, nature and land use, labor, love, and the question of who or what is "English." course_description: American Gothic: from a City on a Hill to the Sunken Place. This course explores the demonizations--literary, legal, political, and alimentary--that haunt America's clearings, those spaces and places in which settler violence and slave labor were so often instrumental. Given that, it makes a great deal of sense to read early American literature for the "gothic effects" that occur when the hard facts of slavery, genocide, misogyny, and food privation merge with utopian fantasies of regeneration, renewal, and abundance for all. With that in mind, we will focus on novels by Charles Brockden Brown, Catharine Maria Sedgwick, Nathaniel Hawthorne, and Stephen King, as well as works by Mary Rowlandson, Edgar Allan Poe, Walt Whitman, Harriet Jacobs, Frederick Douglass, and Emily Dickinson. Along the way, we will watch four films: Stanley Kubrick's cinematic revision of The Shining (1980); Ron Howard's In the Heart of the Sea (2015), a historically-sourced tale of survival at sea through cannibalism; Ryan Coogler's celebration of music in Sinners--particularly the blues--as an archive of Black survival, resistance, and joy (2025); and we will conclude with a viewing of Jordan Peele's exploration of racialized terror lurking within an ostensibly privileged exurban setting in Get Out (2017).Prerequisites: 4 credits at the 100-level in English or third-year standing with instructor permission. course_description: Chaucer is a poet of resistance. A lifelong civil servant who worked in the courts of princes, as part of the governmental bureaucracy and as a Member of Parliament, Chaucer was entrenched in the political debates of his day. Working during the increasingly tyrannical reign of Richard II, Chaucer wrote his Canterbury Tales as a series of stories about and framed within issues of personal and political governance. As we read through the Canterbury Tales, we will focus on Chaucer's representations of gender, power, and bodily diversity as a concerted literary effort to resist the pressures of monarchical government. Drawing parallels between the debates the fourteenth-century England and twenty-first century America, we will see how Chaucer functions as a poet of his time and for our current age. Prerequisite: 8 credits at the 200-level in English; 4 credits must be ENG-204, 210, 215, 223, 224, 225, 226, 227, 228, 229, 230, 231, 232, 240, 273, 274, or 290. ARNER

course_description: Possession and Dispossession. In Shakespeare's Much Ado About Nothing, when Hero, accused of cheating on her fiancé, fakes her death to clear her name, Friar Francis comments on the wisdom of this "strange course" of action, noting that we learn the value of things only when we lose them: "then we find / The virtue that possession would not show us / Whiles it was ours." This research seminar takes an intensive look at possession and dispossession in a selection of Shakespeare's poetry and plays. As we situate these works in their early modern contexts and trace their afterlives in criticism, literature, and performance, we'll also be tracking forms of material, social, erotic, spiritual, and legal possession and dispossession. In many cases, these forms will intersect, as Shakespeare uses the language of one (e.g. slavery) to talk about another (e.g. love). What can representations of possession and dispossession teach us about Renaissance conceptions of the individual and its relation to a changing world? How do characters understand value amidst competing systems of valuation? And how, from the vantage point of our own dynamic era, might these insights shape both our critical habits and our actions? Prerequisite: 8 credits at the 200-level in English; 4 credits must be ENG-204, 210, 215, 223, 224, 225, 226, 227, 228, 229, 230, 231, 232, 240, 273, 274, or 290. EKLUND

course_description: In this course, you will learn many ways of looking at a book as a material object. Often, you will sit down with your classmates to examine a printed text you haven't seen before, and you will work together to understand it. How was it printed and distributed? Who made it, for what audience? What impact did they want it to have? We will undertake that kind of hands-on investigation of American and British texts of many kinds: medieval manuscripts, early newspapers and almanacs, hand-pressed art books, cheap paperbacks, activist underground newspapers, and self-published digital works. In every case, we learn about the people who produced the texts-scribes and early booksellers, Black and feminist activist communities in the 1970s, contemporary digital publishers-and learn about the technological and social tools that connect texts to readers. In addition to scholarly readings and essay assignments, the course will involve creative assignments that encourage students to create their own texts with a range of print and digital technologies. course_description: Advancd Special Topic: Multisensory Imagery. What is lost when we restrict description in a poem to sight-based imagery? A "red barn" is so much more than what our orbs alone can make of it. If the poet has taken the time to describe the barn more fully, we will hear the squawking of a bird on the roof ridge. We will hear the beams themselves whine and crack in the wind. We will feel, as if with our hands, the warped and splintered boards, the fifty-year-old paint peeling like a bad sunburn. We might even smell the pile of dung that sits beside the barn like a pot on the stove. In this three-week course, we will explore how multisensory description can bring the fullness of what we experience to the page. We will learn how to create dynamic images in poems, leaning on the neurological condition (and figure of speech) called synesthesia. Date: Fall meets September 8 to September 24. Spring meets February 23 to March 11. Prerequisite: ENG 205, 206, or 207.

course_description: Special Topic: Environmental Law & Policy. Also listed as PST-295. This course examines how societies govern environmental challenges through the lens of law, policy, and political institutions. Students trace the evolution of environmental governance-from early conservation to modern regulation-exploring the constitutional foundations of administrative authority, property rights, and federalism. The curriculum focuses on the implementation and evaluation of major statutes-such as the Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act, and NEPA-while introducing key economic concepts like externalities, market-based instruments, and environmental justice. By analyzing the trade-offs between economic development and ecological protection, students will learn to assess legitimacy and effectiveness of regulatory frameworks. Through critical engagement with legal and scholarly texts, students will develop the skills to communicate evidence-based arguments regarding contemporary environmental crises. Topics will include: water scarcity and water resource allocation, the impacts of fuel extraction (e.g., "fracking") and agriculture on water quality (e.g., eutrophication), food security and obesity, and the impacts of climate change on the FEWs nexus. The seminar emphasizes close reading of contemporary peer-reviewed literature and includes a major term-writing project. Prerequisite: Open to Junior and Senior Environmental Studies Concentrators.
