system_requisites: EDU-101, two 200-level education course and third-year standing - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: How can education research help hold our society accountable for culturally sustaining and anti-racist practices and promote solutions to educational challenges rather than simply reveal shortfalls? In this advanced seminar for Education Studies Concentrators, we identify the core principles of critical pedagogy and action research and apply them to our research agendas. Each student is supported through scaffolded assignments and collaborative learning to realize a substantive research project on a topic of interest to them. Prerequisite: EDU-101, two 200-level Education course with grade, S, C, or better and third-year standing

system_requisites: None
course_description: See ART-155. This course introduces students to select issues in film studies. Students will learn key vocabulary and concepts of film forms, techniques, and history and develop critical-analysis skills necessary to become informed viewers of a wide variety of historical and contemporary films. Class time will be used for screenings and critical study of major films. Students will produce written critical responses to film, production exercises using consumer tools (smartphones), and a research presentation. Prerequisite: None. TAVARES

system_requisites: Second-year standing - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: See ART-255. This hands-on production course is designed to introduce students to the moving image as a form of contemporary art practice. Students will learn the skills, theories, and concepts used in digital video, participating in all aspects of production, including gathering ideas, writing a project description, storyboarding, shooting, editing, and screening. Students will be exposed to and research a range of moving image artists, gaining an understanding of the history of video art and related forms. Prerequisite: second-year standing. TAVARES

system_requisites: AMS-130, ART-155, or FMS-155 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Also listed as AMS-280. This course examines photography's role in the production of authoritative knowledge about the human body in the U.S. - including by advancing pseudoscientific theories of racial hierarchies, propagating ethnic stereotypes, informing medical diagnoses of the disabled body, delimiting aesthetic ideals for gendered life, and creating spectacles of violence against Black bodies. We will also look at how artists and activists have used the camera as a tool of resistance to resignify marginalized bodies with political power. Prerequisite: AMS-130, ART-155, or FMS-155. REZNICK

system_requisites: None
catalog_notes: Description says: Second-year standing. System Requisites field says None.
course_description: Special Topic: Transnational Women's Cinema. Also listed as ARH-295. In this course, we will unpack "women's cinema" by engaging with how feminist theories, politics, and practices coincide with transnational film production, circulation, and distribution in films made by women filmmakers. We will consider topics such as auteur theory, spectatorship, and representation as we watch films across genres. We will examine the feminist worldbuilding and modes of allyship in women's cinema while paying attention to factors such as race, sexuality, class, caste, nation, and ethnicity. Prerequisite: Second-year standing.

system_requisites: Second-year standing - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Advanced Special Topic: Cinema Spectatorship and Exhibition. Also listed as ARH-395. This course analyzes theories of the cinema spectator, the spectator's relationship to the screen, and the formulation of the spectator through specific media technologies. Students study psychoanalytic, phenomenological, and affective approaches to spectatorship, examine the history of movie exhibition, and consider how individual technologies (television, video, YouTube) shape the spectator's experience and identity. Throughout the course, students develop understandings of spectatorship through written reflections, curating screenings, and developing both individual and group exhibition designs. Prerequisite: Second-year standing.

system_requisites: FRN-101, or by placement of department - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: This course continues the development of communicative competence begun in FRN 101. Through total immersion in the target language, students will learn to use and understand French in real-life situations. All four language areas (speaking, reading, writing, listening) are emphasized. Students will also gain cultural knowledge of the French-speaking world, learning the customs, values, and social practices that accompany the language. Prerequisite: French 101 or by placement. STAFF.

description_prerequisite: FRN-102 or FRN-103; or 200-level placement in French
system_requisites: FRN-102, FRN-103, or 200-level placement in French - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Using contemporary films, television shows, news program, music and other media, this course develops the ability to speak and understand everyday French. Students also develop their cultural knowledge of France and the French-speaking world. The course provides good practice for students preparing to study abroad or complete a French-language internship. May be repeated once for credit. Prerequisite: FRN-102 or FRN-103; or 200-level placement in French.

system_requisites: FRN-102 or FRN-103 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: This course deepens students' linguistic skills alongside their cultural knowledge of the French and Francophone world. While reviewing the essential aspects of French grammar and expanding their vocabulary, students will gain the ability to express increasingly complex thoughts about themselves, others and the world around us, including some of the most pressing contemporary questions-all in French. Prerequisite: French 102 or 103, or placement. STAFF.

system_requisites: FRN-221 or placement - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: This course increases students' communicative and analytical skills in French, focusing on a particular site (such as Paris) or a particular period of history (such as France during the 1960s) to discuss a variety of important texts, films, historical documents, or visual media. The class continues to review and refine students' grammatical skills while enabling students to deepen their cultural understanding, and learn and express more nuances of the French-speaking world. Prerequisite: French 221, or by placement. STAFF.

system_requisites: FRN-222 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: This course focuses on the contemporary French-speaking world and what defines it. It examines the relationship between national identity and the forces of geography, history, language, race, religion, and ethnicity. Topics include: colonization, decolonization, immigration, French-American relations, and societal values related to the family, gender, education, political organization, the state, and secularism. Prerequisite: French 222. STAFF

system_requisites: FRN-222 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: This course examines the love poems, comic novels, family dramas, and philosphical essays that were written in France during the long period that stretches from the Middle Ages to the French Revolution. Students refine their ability to understand the nuances of the French language while also gaining an understanding of French history. Among the many authors studies are Rabelais, Labe, Montaigne, Miliere, Voltaire, and Olympe de Gouges. Prerequisite: French 222. HARRISON.

system_requisites: FRN-312 or 313. - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: This seminar will take us to several Francophone Sub-Saharan African cities to consider the complex ways in which writers and filmakers have portrayed urban Africa. Through texts and films, we will focus on the challenges and possibilities that Africans cities create or deepen. In doing so, we will strive to understand the intersections of different forms of vulnerability, including gender-based, linguistics and economic vulnerabilities, and the role of fiction in giving them a voice. Taught entirely in French. Prerequisite: FRN 312 or 313. TRICOIRE

system_requisites: FRN-312 or 313 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Tragic and Comic Breakups. Using the prism of tragedy and comedy, this seminar will examine why certain literary couples don't stay together. When does a personal flaw rise to the level of tragedy and when is it comical? When can certain breakups be attributed to social pressure, beyond the scope of the couple, and when are they purely the result of individual choices? As we can see, the question of breaking up raises questions about the greater society in which the couple exists-is love merely a passion held by a single person, or is it determined by that person's social background and standing? We'll examine these questions first by looking at a series of seventeenth-century plays written by authors such as Molière, Corneille, and Racine, and then we will work our way to prose fictions of the eighteenth century, where the category of the libertin/e complicates the tragic and comic distinction. Prerequisite: French 312 or 313. HARRISON

system_requisites: None
catalog_notes: Description says: Open to first-year students only. System Requisites field says None.
course_description: The First-Year Experience Course empowers students to develop skills that will contribute to their academic and personal success during their time at Grinnell and beyond. The course provides opportunities for engaging in discussions about personal sustainability, respect, personal and cultural conceptions of identity, living in a diverse community, and using identifying resources. The course helps students learn both how to reflect inward as well as how to have productive conversations across difference. S/D/F grading only. Prerequisite: Open to first-year students only. STAFF

description_prerequisite: one course in Anthropology, or Economics, or Political Science, or Sociology
system_requisites: One course in Anthropology, Economics, Political Science, or Sociology. ECN-111 is strongly recommended. - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: This course adopts an interdisciplinary approach to the analysis of contemporary issues in the economic development of less-developed countries. Course reviews the leading theories of economic, political, and social change that have been adopted by anthropologists, economists, and political scientists, and considers how these theories have shaped past and current debate on the definition and goals of the development process. Course compares and contrasts the approaches adopted by international institutions and alternative development organizations to the "practice" of development. Prerequisite: one course in Anthropology, or Economics, or Political Science, or Sociology. Economics 111 is strongly recommended. BROTTEM, ROPER.

system_requisites: GDS-111 and third-year standing - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Advanced Special Topic: Global Analysis. The topic for spring 2027 is climate change, with a focus on how a warming planet is reshaping conflict, migration, and stability around the world. Our shared text will be The Heat and the Fury: On the Frontlines of Climate Violence by journalist Peter Schwartzstein (Island Press, 2024). We will pay particular attention to how climate change is already reshaping the international community, with particular attention to the developing regions that have contributed least to global emissions yet face the earliest and most severe consequences. Drawing on Schwartzstein's on-the-ground reporting from the Middle East, Africa, and South Asia, we will examine how drought, water scarcity, and resource competition intersect with poverty, governance, and conflict, and what these dynamics mean for international cooperation and development policy going forward. Dates January 25 to March 1. 1/2 semester course deadlines apply. Prerequisite: GDS-111.

system_requisites: None
course_description: Experience daily life in London through regular community engagement, lectures, walking tours, visits to museums, non-profit organizations, and cultural sites around the city and region. Additional field studies will challenge students to learn to navigate London and the broader UK. The course takes an interdisciplinary approach to develop cross-cultural communication skills and each student's sense of belonging in a new space. Prerequisite: None. STAFF.

system_requisites: None
course_description: Women Travel the World: A Feminist Approach to Asian-German Literature. See German 227. This course offers a diverse exploration of Asian-German literature through a feminist approach. We engage the works of authors such as Susanne Hornfeck, Towata Yoku, Anita Desai, and their counterparts, examining how their narratives intersect with gender, identity, and cultural experiences. Topics include but are not limited to migration, diaspora, and belonging, intersecting with critical theories of gender, identity, and world literature. Inviting students to embrace diverse and inclusive voices in the Asian German context through close reading, critical analysis, and class discussions, we aim to foster an appreciation for cross-cultural identity. All texts are in English translation. Prerequisites: None.

description_prerequisite: A course in English or another course in literature
system_requisites: A course in English or another course in literature. - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: See Humanities 251. This course takes a theoretical approach to canonical and contemporary children's texts that deal with constructions of race. It focuses primarily on the history of constructions of race in picture books and a few children's novels. It examines the historical and cultural contexts for the development of African-American children's literature. Prerequisite: A course in English or another course in literature. GREENE

system_requisites: None
course_description: See Russian and Eastern European Studies 291. This course examines and analyzes a number of 20th-century works in translation from several countries of Central and Eastern Europe (primarily, but not limited to the former-Yugoslavia, Poland, and the former-Czechoslovakia). Attention is devoted to how writers, artists, poets, and others attempt to understand and respond to major events and issues in specific countries, and in the region in general: war, genocide, revolution, totalitarianism, political repression, clashes of religion and culture, and quests for (self-)identity. Prerequisite: none. ARMSTRONG.

system_requisites: GRE-101 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Continuation of Greek 101. Review of forms and grammar. Introduction to a range of Greek poetic and prose literature, with selected short readings from Homer, lyric poetry, Herodotus, Sophocles, Euripides, Plato, and the Christian Scriptures. Prerequisite: Greek 101. STAFF.

system_requisites: GRE-222 and HUM-101 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Readings in Greek poetry, excluding Homer and drama. Possibly to include Archaic lyric and elegiac poets (e.g., Sappho, Archilochus, Solon), Pindar and Bacchylides, or the Hellenistic poets (Apollonius, Theocritus, Callimachus). Introduction to Greek metrics and literary dialects. Emphasis on close reading and critical analysis of the texts. Prerequisite: Greek 222 and Humanities 101. STAFF.

system_requisites: GRM-101 - Must be completed prior to taking this course. Take GRM-102L - Must be taken at the same time as this course.
course_description: Continuation and completion of oral-aural study of grammatical structures. Increased emphasis on developing oral fluency. Introduction to the literature and culture of Germany through reading and analysis of modern short stories and expository prose. Practice of oral skills with a native German-speaking assistant. Prerequisite: German 101. STAFF.

system_requisites: None
course_description: No description available.

system_requisites: GRM-221 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: A continuation of GRM 221. This course emphasizes understanding German culture through language, history, literature, popular culture, politics, and the arts. Includes a review of selected topics in German grammar, accompanied and followed by continued practice in speaking, reading, and writing. Prerequisite: German 221. STAFF.

system_requisites: None
course_description: Women Travel the World: A Feminist Approach to Asian-German Literature. Also listed as General Literary Studies 227. This course offers a diverse exploration of Asian-German literature through a feminist approach. We engage the works of authors such as Susanne Hornfeck, Towata Yoku, Anita Desai, and their counterparts, examining how their narratives intersect with gender, identity, and cultural experiences. Topics include but are not limited to migration, diaspora, and belonging, intersecting with critical theories of gender, identity, and world literature. Inviting students to embrace diverse and inclusive voices in the Asian German context through close reading, critical analysis, and class discussions, we aim to foster an appreciation for cross-cultural identity. All texts are in English translation. Prerequisites: none.

system_requisites: TUT-100 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Special Topic: German-Jewish Cultural Map of Shanghai and the Sinophone World. Also listed as EAS-295. This course examines German-Jewish migration, exile, memory, and cultural exchange in Shanghai and the broader Sinophone world. Drawing on literature, memoirs, maps, photographs, archival sources, museums, and film, students explore how German-speaking Jewish refugees interacted within mainland China and the broader Sinophone societies, including Hong Kong, Taiwan, and Singapore,  and how these histories are remembered and represented. Prerequisites: TUT-100

system_requisites: Any 300 level German course. - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Practice in creative writing of fiction, poetry, screen plays, comics, or other media led by the current German Writer in Residence. Close reading and analysis of recent German works from a contemporary cultural perspective. All readings and discussion in German. Prerequisite: Any 300 level German course. May be repeated once for credit. STAFF.

description_prerequisite: GRM-222 or placement in 300 level German course
system_requisites: GRM 222 or placement in 300 level German course - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Advanced Special Topic: Bodies at War: Soldiers, Suffering, and Memory in German Culture. This course examines representations of soldiers, and mothers in German-language literature, film, letters, and other cultural documents from the nineteenth century to the present. Beginning with the disciplined and socially constructed body of the soldier, we will explore how military institutions, class, gender, and ideals of masculinity shape experiences of violence and vulnerability. We will then consider the wounded, traumatized, displaced, and mourning bodies produced by modern warfare and the ways these experiences are communicated through literature, personal testimony, and cultural memory. Throughout the course, we will ask how bodily suffering complicates distinctions among soldiers and civilians, perpetrators and victims, and individual experience and collective memory. Prerequisite: GRM-222 or placement in 300 level German course.

system_requisites: None
course_description: This course introduces students to key topics, concepts, approaches, and problems in Gender, Women's, and Sexuality Studies as the field has developed over the past 45 years. We investigate the significance and meaning of gender at different periods in United States history and explore the development of United States feminism and feminist theory, adopting comparative and transnational perspectives throughout the semester. The ways in which race, ethnicity, sexuality, class, nationality, and age shape experience, culture, ideology, and politics are central areas f inquiry. We also address the means through which women have resisted inequality and affected social and political change. This course takes an interdisciplinary approach, and students are introduced to scholarship from a wide range of disciplines, including cultural studies, economics, history, philosophy, political theory, psychology, and sociology. Prerequisite: none. STAFF

system_requisites: GWS-111 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Special Topic: The Mermaid Imaginary: Race, Gender, and the Global Waters. In this course, we will explore diverse cultural and spiritual traditions of gender formations and waters. Drawing on an interdiscplinary set of academic, literary, artistic texts, we will build an understanding of the "mermaid imaginary" - a rich conceptual space in which cultures have reconsidered their own forms of gender and agency. In the process of uncovering the global significance of mermaid traditions, we will encounter new ways of knowing and being and consider their transformative potential for our living on land. Prerequisite: GWS-111.

system_requisites: GWS-111, AMS-130, or SOC-111 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Special Topic: Critical Disability Studies. This course offers students an overview of critical disability studies from its inception to current debates and possible futures of the field. We will discuss disability's connections to other social categories that, while discursively constructed, profoundly shape individuals' material experiences, including race, ethnicity, gender, sexuality, class, and legal status. Bridging theory, activism, and cultural expression, we will also study intersectional reimaginings of care and healing that address more thoroughly how multiple oppressions structure disabled life. Prerequisites: GWS-111, AMS-130, or SOC-111.

system_requisites: GWS-111 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Special Topic: Feminist Futures, Dystopian Nightmares. This course explores how feminists have used literary and visual narratives to imagine more just futures and to warn of the consequences of a world built on systematic subordination and oppression based on sex, gender identity, race, socio-economic class, religion, disability and other differences that exist among human beings. Students will read classic and contemporary feminist texts that warn of dystopian nightmares where some have lost control of their bodies, natural resources are scarce, governmental corruption has gone unchecked, and/or technology is used unethically. In addition, the course will consider how feminists have used their texts to imagine alternative futures based on humanistic values and equitable systems of governance. Prerequisite: GWS-111.

description_prerequisite: Gender, Women's, and Sexuality Studies 111 and one GWS course at the 200 level
system_requisites: GWS-111 and one 200-level GWS elective course - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: This course provides an introduction to critical theoretical debates about gender, race, and class in the United States legal system. Students examine legal concepts, structures, and narratives that produce and/or reinforce patterns of discrimination and inequality, as well as examine alternative models proposed within critical legal scholarship. Prerequisite: Gender, Women's, and Sexuality Studies 111 and one GWS course at the 200 level. JOHNSON.

description_prerequisite: GWS 111 or EDU 101 and one 200-level course in GWS or EDU
system_requisites: GWS-111 or EDU-101 AND one 200-level course in GWS or EDU - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Also listed as EDU-357. Drawing on education studies, sociology, gender studies, and history, Feminist Educations examines how minoritized genders have encountered and shaped K-12 schooling and post-secondary education over the last 150 years. The course explores the rise of co-education, university campus culture, the feminization of teaching, gender's impact on learning styles, and the ways race, ethnicity, sexuality, gender identity, and social class contribute to students' aspirations and experiences within our deeply gendered learning institutions. Prerequisite: GWS 111 or EDU 101 and one 200-level course in GWS or EDU. BEAUBOEUF

description_prerequisite: senior status; Gender, Women's, and Sexuality Studies Major; Gender, Women's, and Sexuality Studies 111 and 249
system_requisites: GWS-111, 249 and Senior Gender, Women's, and Sexuality Studies major - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: "States of the Field, States of Emergency". Amid rising political repression and heightened harm toward disenfranchised communities, what can gender, sexuality, and feminist studies say about the moment? How might revisiting these fields' foundational lessons, concepts, and frameworks help us understand today's crises? This course overviews the "state of the field." First returning to influential queer, trans, and feminist texts and theories, we will study recent, forthcoming, and cutting-edge scholarship that expands said prior work to address an ever-violent present.Prerequisite: senior status; Gender, Women's, and Sexuality Studies Major; Gender, Women's, and Sexuality Studies 111 and 249. STAFF

system_requisites: None
course_description: Digital History: Local and Global. This course will introduce students to methods used in the digital humanities, with a special emphasis on applications to historical studies. Students will create projects and study existing digital projects, with a special focus on U.S. History in a global context. Readings will include primary sources as well as recent contributions to theory in digital humanities. We will learn general principles of working with humanistic data as well as techniques such as building on-line exhibitions, digital mapping, and computational analysis of text. No technical skills or experience in digital humanities work are required, but willingness to gain both are fundamental to the class. Prerequisite: none. PURCELL

system_requisites: None
course_description: The Prophet Muhammad. This course provides an introduction to issues of historical causation, argumentation, and evidence, by exploring the life and impact of the prophet Muhammad on the Arabian Peninsula and West Asia in the early seventh century. We will begin with an introduction to the study of history and historical methods. From there, we will read a variety of primary and secondary sources in order to answer the question: Who was the Prophet Muhammad? Prerequisite: none. SABA

system_requisites: None
course_description: The Historian as Detective. History is a form of detective work. Historians arrive after the event. They look for traces and clues left behind. They study the evidence closely. They ask about motive and circumstance. They pay attention to gaps and silences in the record. This class introduces students to the craft of historical inquiry by treating the historian as an investigator of the global past. We will read fiction, classic works of history, and primary sources related to "true crimes", disputes, mutinies, and other contested events in the last two hundred years. Students will work to reconstruct what happened, why it happened, and what these events meant to the people who experienced them. Along the way, students will learn how to decipher historical records, explain cause and effect, understand what archives are, how information is produced and circulated, and appreciate how larger historical contexts shape everyday life. Prerequisite: None. STAFF.

system_requisites: HIS-100 or second-year standing - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: A general survey of Latin American history from the Columbian encounter through Independence. The course will focus on the patterns of European conquest and colonization, the complexity of race relations in the region, and the problems of colonial administration. Prerequisite: History 100 or second-year standing. SILVA.

system_requisites: HIS-100, or second-year standing - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Also listed as AMS 215. Students in this course will examine the creation and expansion of U.S. popular culture in the nineteenth century as they focus on diverse cultural forms: dime novels, newspapers, music, sports, cartoons, theater, minstrel shows, magazines, etc. The course will focus particularly on how ideas and structures of race, class, and gender were changed and reinforced by American popular culture and will consider theoretical issues involved in the study of popular culture. Prerequisite: HIS-100 or second-year standing. PURCELL

system_requisites: HIS-100 or second-year standing - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: From the end of treaty-making with the United States in the late-nineteenth century through to the present, this course examines the struggles of Native peoples in tribal sovereignty while simultaneously acknowledging connections to the United States. Focusing on some well-known events and people, like Little Big Horn and Geronimo, and many lesser-known people and events, this course examines persistence and change as American Indians in the United States grappled with issues of sovereignty and citizenship. Prerequisite: HIS-100 or second-year standing.

system_requisites: HIS-100 or second-year standing - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: A survey of the African-American experience in slavery and freedom, with a primary emphasis on the struggle for racial justice and equality since the Civil War. Assignments stress primary sources as well as scholarly studies, films, and recordings. Prerequisite: History 100 or second-year standing. LACSON.

system_requisites: HIS-100 or second-year standing - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Covering approximately 1000-1600 CE, this course will chart the transformation of medieval Christendom, the emergence of a new Europe, and its explosion outward into the wider early modern world. Prerequisite: History 100 or second-year standing. STAFF

system_requisites: HIS-100 or second-year standing - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: This course examines the everyday lives of people in the "germanic lands" from roughly the sixteenth through the late nineteenth centuries. What did it mean to be "German" in central Europe before the official founding in 1871 of the modern nation-state? We consider daily practices and local traditions both on the continent and in immigrant communities, borrowing from scholars of material culture studies and Alltagsgeschichte. Through close readings and hands-on work with texts and objects, we will study language and printing, foodways, weaving and embroidery, musical and visual cultures, and engagement with the land to explore the lived experience of Germans before Germany. Prerequisite: History 100 or second-year standing. MAYNARD.

description_prerequisite: One 100-level "Studying Religion" course, HIS-100, or second-year standing
system_requisites: one 100-level "Studying Religion" course, HIS-100, or second-year standing - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: See REL-285. This course will use the work of 12th century scholar Ibn Rushd (Averroes) as a window into the theory and historical practice of Islamic law. We will cover a range of specific topics including criminal law, family law, inheritance law, and the laws of war. The class will also study how this legal system has been implemented across time, debates surrounding the questions of gender, and the contested place of religion in modern legal systems. Foreign language option in Arabic available for students who do the Plus-2 option. Prerequisite: One 100-level "Studying Religion" course, HIS-100, or second-year standing. SABA

system_requisites: HIS 100 or second-year standing - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: This course explores questions about how we make meaning through craft. How have craftspeople grappled with the social and political problems of their times? In what ways has crafting served as an alternative archive, as a tool for resistance, community, ritual, privilege, or appropriation? How has craft articulated identities and challenged normative paradigms? Together we examine case studies across the globe and pieces in clay, textiles, and wood. Students work on individual crafting and complete small-scale research projects. Dates: Fall section 01 August 31 to October 15. Spring section 01 January 25 to March 10. Prerequisite: HIS-100 or second-year standing.

system_requisites: One 4-credit 100 or 200-level Grinnell History course - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Scholars agree that the development of capitalism was important, but disagree about how it came about. We will look at some classic works that started this debate, some contributions of the 1970s and 1980s that revived it, as well as a few more contemporary interventions. Through our discussions, students should acquire some workable definitions of capitalism, some plausible explanations for its emergence, and some insights into how different disciplines formulate arguments about such fundamental questions. Prerequisite: One 4-credit 100 or 200-level Grinnell History course.

system_requisites: HIS-100 or second-year standing - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Special Topic: The World of the Crusades. In this course students will learn about the major "numbered" crusades, especially the First Crusade through the Fourth. But they will also learn about the world of the crusades. Students will encounter the world as it was prior to the movement's inception, explore how it came about and evolved, and look at how the wider world and subsequent events were shaped by crusade ideas and practices. This class will not focus solely on the Latin Christian crusaders and their world. To be sure, students will learn about Latin Christendom and its expansion into so-called "crusader states" of Edessa, Antioch, Jerusalem, and Tripoli. But students will also learn about the Byzantines, the Seljuk Turks, Fatimid Egypt, the Taifa kingdoms of al-Andalus, and the Almoravid and Almohad regimes of the Maghrib. We will also explore how the crusades did and did not continue after the fall of the last Latin polity in the Levant, how crusading shaped subsequent European encounters with Africa and the Americas, and how crusading has been remembered in subsequent centuries, including in the modern era.Prerequisite: HIS-100 or second-year standing.

system_requisites: Second-year standing - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: London: The Mysterious Metropolis. Also listed as Humanities 295. History is like detective work. This class will "inspect" the modern history of London through its mysteries: real and imagined, solved and unsolved. From Victorian fascinations with Sherlock Holmes and Jack the Ripper to trials of imperial misdeeds in the High Court, Londoners have used modern narrative and investigative techniques to chase criminals, expose crimes, and tell truths. We will explore these stories through fiction, media, theatre, and excursions around London's historical and contemporary cityscape. Prerequisite: Second-year standing. PREVOST.

system_requisites: TUT-100 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Special Topic: Soccer and the African Diaspora. Cross-list ADS-295. Soccer was first introduced in Africa in the nineteenth century at the height of European colonialism. Despite this context, soccer in Africa and among the African diaspora has taken on a life of its own worthy of study. This course traces how soccer evolved from a tool of colonial discipline to a site of anti-colonial resistance. We will examine how soccer (as sport, community, and industry) constitutes an analytic tool for understanding how African diaspora communities engaged imperialism, nationalism, decolonization, and identity. Prerequisite: TUT-100

system_requisites: HIS-100 or second-year standing - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Special Topic: Reading the French Revolution. This is a reading-intensive course exploring the historiography of the French Revolution. Beyond classic political and economic debates, our focus is on recent scholarship centering questions like: What roles did women play during the many phases of the revolution? How did the lived experience of everyday people generate ideas of universalism, collective identity, or renewed faith? What was the relationship between events in France and the Haitian Revolution, and what did Haiti's success mean for subsequent understandings of "Frenchness"? What insight might the end of the Terror offer for understanding other radical social movements? How did the experience of Napoleonic military service impact "fraternity" and male sexualities? We foreground discussion, collaboration, comparison, and analysis rather than individual research and writing tasks. Prerequisite: HIS-100 or second-year standing.

system_requisites: HIS 100 and HIS 201 or HIS 202 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: As the saying goes, Latin America lies too far from God and too close to the United States. This proximity has affected Latin American economics, demographics, culture, and politics. The seminar will begin with common readings. This year those common readings will focus on US attempts--both official and unofficial--to democratize and modernize the region. Students will then write a research paper using primary documents. These papers could focus on any one of a number of issues that were central to US-Latin American relations such as hemispheric security, economic affairs, democracy, and socialism. A reading knowledge of Spanish or Portuguese is helpful but not required. Prerequisite: HIS-100 and History 201 or 202.

description_prerequisite: HIS-100 and one of HIS-232 HIS-295 World of the Crusades, HIS-295 God/Empire/Medieval World or HIS-295 Florence/Dante/Machiavelli
system_requisites: HIS 100 and one of HIS-232, HIS-295 World of the Crusades, HIS-295 God/Empire/Medieval World or HIS-295 Florence/Dante/Machiavelli - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Between the fall of the Roman Empire and the sixteenth century era of the Protestant and Catholic Reformations, what we now know as Europe was instead best understood as Latin Christendom, a world in which a shared sense of religious identity, institutions, and practices created an "us" far more robust than any other marker of shared identity, at least for the majority of the population. But medieval Christianity was not a simple or a homogenous thing during these long centuries. Instead, it was complex, constantly evolving, and frequently contested. Students in this seminar will examine key themes in the historiography of this large and complex field of study and pursue research projects on any topic related to it. Such topics might include but are not limited to the medieval papacy, monasticism, women's religious experiences, saints, heresy and the inquisition, crusading, or any of a range of medieval religious ideas and practices, as well as their innumerable intersections with other aspects of medieval life, for example politics and warfare, economic activity and the law, or sexuality and the family. Prerequisite: HIS-100 and one of HIS-232 HIS-295 World of the Crusades, HIS-295 God/Empire/Medieval World or HIS-295 Florence/Dante/Machiavelli

description_prerequisite: Any 200 level HIS course or a course from the Core Area Requirements (Language & Culture, and History, Religion and Society) of the EAS concentration
system_requisites: Any 200 level HIS course or a course from the Core Area Requirements (Language & Culture, and History, Religion and Society) of the EAS concentration. - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Civilizations do not clash; empires do. This seminar explores the history of U.S.-East Asian relations from the nineteenth century to the present day, beginning with the U.S. entrance into Asia as a colonial power and end with the legacy of the Cold War. It juxtapose the perspectives, interests, and arguments of U.S. and East Asian actors to understand this social, political and cultural history. This seminar investigates the global dimension of U.S.-Asian interactions: how did transnational and international forces between U.S. and Asian societies and governments shape key dynamics of the global twentieth century? Why was there unprecedented support for U.S. overseas expansion in this period? And how did U.S. and Asian migrants, lobbyists, NGOs and other private actors develop a sustained impact on global politics? Prerequisites:Any 200 level HIS course or a course from the Core Area Requirements (Language & Culture, and History, Religion and Society) of the EAS concentration.

system_requisites: None
course_description: A foundation for further study in the liberal arts, developing skills of critical reading, writing, and imaginative thinking through the study of selected works from ancient Greece. Readings include Homeric epic, tragic drama, Platonic dialogues, Thucydides' History and Aristotle's Poetics. Prerequisite: none. STAFF.

system_requisites: None
course_description: Major works of Roman and early Christian culture, exploring private and public paths to happiness from Cicero's ideal commonwealth to the City of God. Readings include Virgil's Aeneid, Stoic and Epicurean philosophy, satire and drama, Christian scripture, St. Augustine, and Boethius. Emphasis on close reading, discussion, and short essay assignments. Prerequisite: none. STAFF.

description_prerequisite: a course in English or another course in literature
system_requisites: A course in English or another course in literature - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Also listed as General Literary Studies 251. This course takes a theoretical approach to canonical and contemporary children's texts that deal with constructions of race. It focuses primarily on the history of constructions of race in picture books and a few children's novels. It examines the historical and cultural contexts for the development of African-American children's literature. Prerequisite: a course in English or another course in literature. Greene

system_requisites: Second-year standing - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: London: The Mysterious Metropolis. Also listed as HIS-295. History is like detective work. This class will "inspect" the modern history of London through its mysteries: real and imagined, solved and unsolved. From Victorian fascinations with Sherlock Holmes and Jack the Ripper to trials of imperial misdeeds in the High Court, Londoners have used modern narrative and investigative techniques to chase criminals, expose crimes, and tell truths. We will explore these stories through fiction, media, theatre, and excursions around London's historical and contemporary cityscape. Prerequisite: Second-year standing. PREVOST.

system_requisites: TUT-100 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Special Topic: Postcolonial African Literature in Translation. Also listed as ADS-295 and SAM-295. In this course, we will read some of the most vibrant French-language literature from the African continent in English translation, including foundational "classics" and the contemporary novels of our times, retracing some of the hopes, struggles, and issues that have marked postcolonial Africa. Away from stereotypical and incomplete images and reports, we will delve into the creative potential of fiction to help us think about memory, loss, feminism, family, migration, and more. Prerequisite: TUT-100

system_requisites: Second-year standing _____ *** This course is offered online through the School of Public Health at the University of Iowa. *** _____ If you register for this course, you must also submit the Application to Enroll in Fundamentals of Public Health for Spring 2022 found at: https://bit.ly/2zha8ga - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: *** This 3-credit course is offered online through the School of Public Health at the University of Iowa. *** To register for this course, you must submit the Application to Enroll in Fundamentals of Public Health found under the Student heading on the Registrar's SharePoint site: https://grinco.sharepoint.com This course will provide students with an introduction to the field of public health. Students will be introduced to key disciplines, methods, and topics in public health practice and research. Foundational concepts used throughout the course include social determinants of health, health equity, behavioral theories and epidemiological methods. Lectures will cover a wide range of current public health topics, including infectious disease, maternal and child health, agricultural health, health policy, and indigenous health. Students will also hear from graduate students in public health and explore career options in public health. Course Objectives By the end of this course, students should be able to: 1) Identify the differences between population-based health and individual-based health 2) Describe how scientific evidence is utilized to develop public health practices and interventions 3) Describe the major disciplines in public health 4) Describe the various career paths in public health 5) Explain the major achievements of public health, including the impact they have had on the health of the population 6) Apply creative problem solving strategies to address specific issues in public health 7) Describe future challenges for public health in the 21st century. _____ The course follows a weekly schedule roughly parallel to our semester schedule and typically involves watching recorded lectures, reading, on-line discussions with other students and the instructor, three papers (3-5 pages), and four exams.

system_requisites: None
course_description: This discussion-based, interdisciplinary Latin American studies course approaches "culture" broadly to include a wide spectrum of everyday experiences, and provides students with a solid foundation for subsequent academic work in the region. The course begins with an overview of definitions of "Latin America" and of its current state as an object of interdisciplinary study and then explores contemporary issues (i.e. state repression, human rights, immigration) via various disciplines (humanities and social sciences) and genres (i.e. academic essays, narrative journalism, testimonio). Prerequisites: none. APARICIO, BENOIST.

system_requisites: LAT-103 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Continuation of Latin 103. Readings in classical Latin prose and poetry, with review and composition as needed in order to attain a reading knowledge of Latin. Prerequisite: Latin 103. M. CUMMINS, MERCADO.

system_requisites: LAT-222 and HUM-101 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: The poetry of Lucretius and some of the essays of Cicero will be studied for the ways in which they present Greek ideas to a Roman audience, on the subjects of nature, religion, politics, and the goals of life. Prerequisite: Latin 222 and Humanities 101. J. CUMMINS.

system_requisites: None
course_description: What is language and how is it studied scientifically? This survey course introduces the core subfields of linguistics - phonetics, phonology, morphology, syntax, and semantics - and how these areas integrate with one another in the study of language and society, language acquisition, language technologies, and language change. Our goal is to determine what it means to 'know' a language and to examine how language is acquired, produced, and processed, and with what social effects. Prerequisite: None. STAFF.

system_requisites: LIN-114 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

In this course, students will learn to evaluate what is unusual and what is expected in a language. We will determine the range of possible sound inventories, word order patterns, grammatical categories, and lexical categories found within the world's languages. Prerequisite: LIN-114.

We will also compare different theories of loanword adaptation and consider how different linguistic and social contexts affect the outcome of borrowing. Prerequisite: LIN-114 with grade S, C, or better. GLEWWE

What is learned about functions is then applied to topics in modeling, such as linear regression, difference equations, mixed models, the logistic equation, and probability. Prerequisite: None.

Additional topics may include applications to differential equations, line integrals, and Green's Theorem. Prerequisite: Mathematics 124 or 131. STAFF.

course_description: See Computer Science 208. How do we "know" that a mathematical or logical statement is correct? What common properties appear among different collections? How might we represent functions, and how can we tell if two functions with different representations are the same? Can we formally describe and understand common diagrams? We consider such questions as we develop both intuition and formal mechanisms for addressing them. Along the way, we explore Boolean logic, proof techniques, sets, structures that include trees and graphs, and more Students who are taking or have previously taken Math 218 may not take Computer Science/Math 208. Prerequisite: Computer Science 151 and Math 124 or 131, and completion of or concurrent registration in Computer Science 161. STAFF.

system_requisites: MAT-133 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Linear algebra plays a fundamental role in mathematics and its applications. From a computational perspective, the subject studies systems of linear equations and matrix algebra. Some courses include additional applications such as fitting lines and curves to data, Markov processes, and linear differential equations. From a more abstract perspective, linear algebra studies linear transformations between vector spaces. This course balances the computational, conceptual, and theoretic aspects of the subject, and explores their connections. In addition to the core topics (matrices, vector spaces, eigenvectors, dimension), the course develops mathematical reasoning and writing skills. Prerequisite: Mathematics 133. STAFF.

system_requisites: MAT-215 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Elementary Number theory is one of the oldest branches of mathematics, far older than Calculus. The subject, at its most basic, asks questions about the integers. For instance, how are the prime numbers distributed among the integers? What are integer solutions to a particular polynomial equation? Which integers can be expressed as the sum of two squares? We will learn about topics such as divisibility, congruences, and quadratic reciprocity, which will help us answer questions like these. Along the way, we will discuss counting techniques and related discrete topics. Proof writing and creative problem solving will be heavily emphasized. Prerequisite: Mathematics 215. STAFF.

system_requisites: MAT-215 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Linear algebra is the study of linear equations, vectors and matrices, and linear transformations. Tools from linear algebra are utilized in basically all branches of mathematics, and linear systems arise in many real-world situations, ranging from modeling in physics to machine learning to weather forecasting. This second course in linear algebra will build on what students learned in Math 215. Topics will include vector spaces over arbitrary fields, inner products, orthogonality, matrix decompositions, and the spectral theorem. We will also focus on improving proof-writing and problem-solving skills throughout the term. This course is a great fit for students interested in pure or applied math as well as students interested in physics, computer science, or other disciplines that utilize tools from linear algebra. Prerequisite: MAT-215. HAZEL

system_requisites: MAT-215 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: First and second order differential equations; series solutions and Fourier series; linear and nonlinear systems of differential equations; applications. Prerequisite: Mathematics 215. STAFF.

system_requisites: MAT-220 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: An introduction to the process and techniques of modeling 'real-world' situations, using topics from linear algebra and differential equations. Appropriate mathematics, including numerical methods, developed when needed. Models drawn from both the social and natural sciences. Prerequisite: Mathematics 220. STAFF.

system_requisites: MAT-313 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Advanced Mathematical Methods for Biological Science. This course provides an introduction to mathematical biology, exploring how discrete and continuous models describe the movement and interaction of biological systems across space and time. Students will learn to derive and solve partial differential equations (PDEs) to understand phenomena such as the spread of invasive species, tumor growth, and cellular signaling. The curriculum covers the Turing mechanisms behind pattern formation, as well as the analytical and numerical simulation of reaction-diffusion equations. By focusing on practical applications in ecology and epidemiology, students develop the mathematical and computational tools necessary to analyze how spatial variability influences the natural world. Additionally, students will implement these biological models using Python or MATLAB. Prerequisite: MAT-313.

system_requisites: MAT-218 or 222 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: A thorough study of the topology of the real line and of limits of functions of one real variable. This theory is then used to develop the theory of the derivative and integral of functions of one real variable and also sequences and series of real numbers and functions. Prerequisite: Mathematics 218, or 222. STAFF.

system_requisites: MAT-321 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

We then apply this machinery to study many problems, some of which date back to the ancient Greeks. The techniques used to solve these problems have largely defined the modern approach to Algebra. Prerequisite: MAT-321.

system_requisites: MAT/STA-335 - Must be completed prior to taking this course.

Topics will include: principles of estimation and hypothesis testing, chi-square tests, linear models including regression and analysis of variance, and nonparametric inference. A variety of applications will be considered. Prerequisite: Mathematics/Statistics 335. STAFF.

While the use of computers has changed our world in many respects, this has not (with few exceptions) come back to help mathematicians in their research. This course will show how computers can be used to solve a variety of problems from calculus, linear algebra, combinatorics, analysis, and other areas. The common thread is using the computer for discovery, not just calculations. Students will master a computer algebra system, learn some recently developed algorithmic tools, and work on a research project. The course is intended for anyone interested in seeing how computers can be used to solve problems in pure mathematics. Recommended for those considering graduate school in mathematics. Previous experience with a computer algebra system is not required. Prerequisite: MAT-316. MAT-321 is recommended.

Attention is focused on music-making as a form of human activity within and between cultures. Course content ranges over musics of diverse times and places. No prior experience in music is needed. course_description: Introductory Special Topic: Zimbabwean Dance and Ritual as Liberation Practice. Also listed as THD-195. This three-week course offers students an immersive introduction to Zimbabwean dance as a cultural practice deeply rooted in community, history, ritual, and social change. Students will explore dance as a powerful vehicle for cultural expression, knowledge transmission, and collective transformation. Through Zimbabwean dance, music, song, and a deeper understanding of the ritual practices that accompany them, students will gain insight into Zimbabwean cultural value systems. The course emphasizes how dance reflects and shapes resistance practices. Prerequisite: None. Dates: April 26 to May 12. Short course deadlines apply.

system_requisites: None
course_description: "This course examines the relationship between music and language, the two domains defining us uniquely human. What are the possible origins of music and language? What are the commonalities and differences between them? Is music a universal language, or is it even a language at all? How are musicality and linguisticity associated with each other? In what ways could music and language be said to have meaning? Is musical meaning intrinsic or extrinsic? What is the process by which musical meaning is created and communicated? How can awareness of music's linguistic and discursive nature help us understand and explain its meaning? To answer questions like these, we will draw on a range of disciplines-from music theory to music history and ethnomusicology, from linguistics to semiotics, and from evolutionary biology to neuroscience." Prerequisite: None.

course_name: Topics in Am Music: Queer Pop!
system_requisites: None
course_description: Queer orientations in popular music can work to form bonds based on similar lived experiences, while reaching audiences outside of the LGBTQIA+ community. But what makes queer music special, and how is queer music interacting with its intended (and unintended) audiences? This course uses queer pop, broadly defined, as a site for examining issues of community, chosen family, queer joy, desire, and music reception in various contexts to better understand the music and the people who love it. From everything from Lil Nas X, to drag queens and kings, to Chappell Roan, this course teaches the tools to engage with and analyze this music through various lenses while maintaining the joy found within it. Prerequisites: none

system_requisites: Second-semester standing. - Must be completed prior to taking this course.
course_description: Ubuntu: Philosophy, Performance, and Community in Zimbabwe (and Iowa). Ubuntu, common in several languages across Southern and Eastern Africa, is a philosophical concept that can be translated as "a moral sense of personhood." In this course we explore ubuntu as a moral philosophy, social ethic, and artistic value in embodied ways. We will read, discuss, and play music with one another throughout the term, both at Grinnell and in Zimbabwe. We reflect on how ubuntu can contribute to the common good, make our choices as musicians, community members, and social actors more considerate of others and grounded philosophically. More specifically, we will consider how ubuntu (locally known as hunhu) is understood in Zimbabwe and informs life there. We also embody the lessons of ubuntu through shared musicking and dancing in Shona idioms from Zimbabwe. In order to fully embody a Zimbabwean sense of hunhu, we will travel to the Ubuntu Learning Village in central Zimbabwe over spring break, where we will live our lives according to ubuntu principles and learn lessons in food, community, music, and dance. A semester-long framing device considers how centering ubuntu can contribute to a broad-based liberal arts curriculum in ways that avoid reliance an Cartesian dualism, Enlightenment philosophy, or Eurocentrism. As Desmond Tutu says, "a person is only a person through others." Prerequisites: Second-semester standing. course_description: Topics in Sonic Creativity: Sounds of Peace and Conflict. How are soundscapes of peace and conflict signifying socio-political contention globally? Do these sounds give meaning to negotiations of nation-states? What do the sounds of mythology and cosmology tell us about how humans relate to identity and cultural character? This course affords students an opportunity to develop their listening skills as they contextualize to their positionalities within a global milieu. Students will create their own soundscapes of place and curate ideas of peace and conflict through presentations of collective ephemerality. And although soundscapes of peace and conflict cannot be prophetic, attuning to them allows us to begin a multi-sensorial inquiry into confirmations of personhood, cultural tension, and performing tolerance. Prerequisite: MUS-100 or second-year standing.

course_description: In this seminar we will engage in a careful study of the work of Ludwig Wittgenstein. Wittgenstein's thought is typically divided into three periods--the early (Tractatus), middle (The Blue and Brown Books) and late (Philosophical Investigations and On Certainty)--and we will examine his views in the philosophy of language, the philosophy of mind, metaphysics and epistemology in each of them. Particular attention will be paid to the continuities and discontinuities in his views across these periods as well as the broader philosophical motivations for and consequences of them. Majors themes and topics that will be focused on include: From the early period: The notion of logical form and the picture theory of meaning, the nature of the proposition and the analysis of generality, the limits of sense and the saying/showing distinction; From the middle period: The color-exclusion problem and the idea of language as a calculus of rules or conventions; From the late period: the notion of language games and the use 'theory' of meaning, the rule-following considerations, the argument against the possibility of a private language, philosophy-as-therapy and the dissolution of skepticism. For the 2020-21 academic year this course will be split into two 2-credit terms. Prerequisite: Philosophy 253, 254, 256, 257, or 258. FENNELL
